title: Segregated school in Xenia and learning to find do
summary: He attended a colored school though he could have gone to the white one; a visiting singing teacher, Miss McCarthy, taught do-re-mi which he used to find the key on his horn.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: How were the schools in Xenia?
Segregated. Mostly... No, I could have gone to the... I could have gone to the White school, because I lived out of the corporation(?); I lived in the County, you
know. So I could have had my choice. But my school was close to home and everything, so I went... It was strictly a Colored school I went to. So...

No, not really. There was a singer teacher who used to come up there from down at the White school. Her name was Miss McCarthy. And she'd come and, you know, would teach us singing, like, you know, Do-Re-Me-Fa-Sol-La-Te-Do; E-G-B-D-F. I didn't pay any mind to the E-G-B-D-F thing; you know, the (?) like that. Do-Re-Me-Fa-Sol-La-Te-Do was easy for me, so that's the way I learned, you know. So I pulled(?) my sounds like that, and then out of my horn, that's where I... Wherever "do" was at, if it was in the key of E-flat or whatever; all I had to do was find "do," and I could find the rest of it. It came pretty easy for me. I don't know why, but... All I want to know is where is "do." I can play the rest of whatever it is.
Did anybody ever teach you the positions and all that stuff?

There's a guy who taught me where "do" was at... You know, I later found out that it was the key of B-flat. But at the time, Do-Re-Me-Fa-Sol-La-Te-Do; that's what he said, you know. So I could do that in any key, you know. So that made the pieces easy unless they changed keys
